title: For those who've built a game with AI agents, what was harder than you expected?
author: Any_Inevitable_4035
selftext:
I'm working on my first game, a small 2D stealth thing in Unity. Getting the systems working with an AI agent went faster than I expected, but tuning how they feel took most of my time. Guard reaction timing, how loud footsteps should be, that kind of thing.

What surprised you? Was it the code, the feel, art consistency, or something else?

comments.author: Snownova
comments.body:
Currently my biggest struggle is sound design. I'm the kind of player who has game sound on very low and watches youtube on the second monitor, so it's never been a priority for me, but I'm self-aware enough to know that most people do enjoy games having sound and even music :)

Another thing was keeping AI generated assets consistent in style and coloration. It took bouncing back between GPT generating the art and Claude applying filters for consistent style to finally get it right.

Managing token usage was also something I wish I paid more attention to at the start. I just did a major overhaul of my documentation and claude.md that significantly dropped my token usage, so I shouldn't run out of my weekly usage in 4 days again.

replies.author: MrShaitan
replies.body:
I’ve had a lot of success with sound design by connecting Claude to ElevenLabs. I had to get the 99$ a year membership but now I can describe the general style of sound effect I want, ask Claude to go through the entire game and list every sound I’ll need with a prompt that matches my style preference, and it’ll use elevenlabs to generate several variations of each sound. I was able to do every sound in my game in about 90 min. 

Managing tokens has been a major problem though, what exactly did you do to mitigate it?

replies.author: Snownova
replies.body: Yes! I just signed up with Elevenlabs as well, mostly because I wanted to use their text to speech function and they have a lot of voices with accents which I wanted for my game, but then I found they can generate sounds from prompts too, at a fraction of the token cost, I prioritised those.

replies.author: Snownova
replies.body:
As for token usage, I asked Claude:

>I seem to be burning through my tokens rather fast this week. Do you know why and can you suggest any improvements to our workflow to save on token usage?

It turned out that my claude.md and several of my project documentation files had gotten rather large, so claude proposed to to the following:

1. Cut CLAUDE.md to standing rules, about 15–20 KB. Keep where things live, how you work (git, doclock, TODO, tests), the writing rules and the interface rules. Replace the long sections ("Screen decisions in brief", "World and lore", "Game design decisions", much of "Code") with one-line pointers like "Fleet: see screens/28". The details are already in those docs. This alone saves around 35k tokens per session.

2. Change the ark-record-decision skill so design decisions go only into their owning doc. CLAUDE.md would get a line only when a rule about how to work changes. Otherwise the file will just grow back.

3. Add a reading rule to CLAUDE.md: never read a doc over about 50 KB in full; grep for the key or heading and read only that section.

4. Split messages-and-assignments.md by arc (EG, ARCH, PLG, FLT, EARTH, Library entries), and maybe technology.md by tier. The importer would need to read several files, but sessions would load only the arc they work on.

5. Run fewer agents at once, and keep sessions short. Each agent pays the startup cost, and a long session re-sends its growing history on every turn. One prompt per session, started fresh, is cheaper than a long session doing several prompts.

6. Take screenshots sparingly. Each image costs about 1,500 tokens or more, so comparing against the Amber renders over many rounds adds up. One screenshot at the end of a fix is usually enough.

7. Ask quick questions outside the Ark project when they don't need it. Inside the project, even a one-line question loads the whole CLAUDE.md.

Ark is the working name of the project. I kind of ignored numbers 5 and 7, but after asking claude to implement the rest I've seen a marked drop in token usage.

replies.author: Overwatcher_Leo
replies.body:
LLMs are no good with sounds. So I just used an existing sfx collection from an asset store. There are some pretty good and large ones. The agent is not good at choosing the right ones, so I also had it include a devtool where I can pick and mix sounds from that collection.

Don't try to shoehorn ai agents into every task. It's a tool, and a versatile one at that, but it can't do everything.

comments.author: hydroxyHU
comments.body: I was struck by just how difficult it was to ensure the cohesion of the game’s features. Claude writes code that works functionally and backs it up with unit and end-to-end tests, but he wasn’t able to properly assess whether this was actually visible to the player, whether it was understandable, transparent, or even correct. I’d planned to make a historical castle defence game based on Frostpunk’s morality system and decision-making, whilst also incorporating my own economic engine. At first, everything was fine and dandy, but then the whole thing started to fall apart. I had to start chipping away at the unnecessary bits, playtest after playtest. It didn’t help that Claude tends to work in fits and starts from time to time – he might miss a thing or two here and there – but even in the short term, the breakneck pace of development means things can very quickly become unmanageable. Now, two months on, I’ve switched to a smaller-scale game, and I’ll probably have to start my original idea all over again.

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
For me it was that the agent is too willing to fix things. Describe a bug and it will happily add a special case for exactly that situation, and a few weeks later you have five little patches doing overlapping jobs that nobody remembers adding. I'd get in the habit of asking it to remove something whenever it adds a fix, or at least to explain what the existing code was meant to do before it touches it.



On your tuning point, I'd pull all the feel numbers (reaction delay, noise radius, footstep volume) into one data file or ScriptableObject early, so you can tweak them yourself in play mode instead of going through the agent for every 0.1s change.

replies.author: crackedpotstudio
replies.body: When working with claude, put effort mode on low, it will ask a lot more questions instead of wandering off on it’s own and implement stuff you didn’t ask for.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797
replies.body: Huh, I'd have guessed the opposite, that low effort just makes it rush ahead. Does it still stop to ask on bigger changes, or mostly on the small ones?

replies.author: crackedpotstudio
replies.body:
In general it ask on both changes, I initially thought the same as you but I learned from Reddit it's a whole lot more than that and nicely explained in the claude [documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) . But you're basically telling Claude how much effort and how much it should think for itself with the effort mode. So when giving small and clear instructions in low effort mode it will be much more tempted to stick with that single task and ask for your input when anything is unclear. When putting it on max mode you're basically telling claude ''Do the best thing you can come up with and think as hard as you can about it'' resulting in him going ''off'' a lot more and trying to come up with this huge elaborate tasks that he thinks will improve everything altogether.

I mainly use the higher effort modes when coming up with a basic idea or try to pull up a quick tech demo on a brainfart and let him really think about the baseline, after that I switch to low effort mode and start tackling things 1 by 1.

replies.author: No-Pollution7797

comments.author: BuildMyClub
comments.body:
The biggest challenge I’ve encountered with agentic coding isn’t writing code from scratch—it’s agile development on complex, evolving systems.

Throughout my career, my favorite projects have been long-term systems that morph over years into something entirely different. I’ve watched a single monolithic app evolve into a decoupled API and frontend, add a mobile layer, migrate from XML to REST and now GraphQL, and shift from direct payment gateways to syncing carts and products via Shopify. What the system is today looks nothing like it did ten years ago.

When I tried bringing that same exploratory, evolving approach to my personal projects using agentic coding, I hit a wall. Don't get me wrong—the technology is phenomenal. But agents struggle to conceptualize architectural evolution: taking a system that works one way and shifting its underlying logic to work another.

Git history can tell an agent what changed, and hierarchical folder structures (like Interpretable Context Methodology) help feed it a concise snapshot without blowing out the context window. But neither effortlessly captures why the system behaves the way it does—the subtle nuances and seemingly unconventional technical decisions that are actually critical to keeping the whole thing standing.

Because agents degrade as their context fills up, you’re constantly spinning up fresh sessions and recontextualizing from scratch. And when an agent looks at a localized piece of code that intentionally breaks a standard pattern for the sake of the broader system, its instinct is to "fix" it.

People call this agentic drift, but I think it’s simpler than that: agents optimize for local patterns, while senior engineers optimize for systemic intent.

If you don't understand the lower-level architecture of what you’re building—your database constraints, schema trade-offs, and ingestion pipelines—iteratively refactoring with agents will eventually leave you with baffling bugs you can't trace. Context windows will inevitably grow, and the tooling will catch up. Until then, agile, evolving software still depends entirely on talented engineers holding the guardrails.

replies.author: DetectiveWorking5512
replies.body:
I guess you could more accurately say that I used Gemini to better build/drive the generator, using python scripts to prompt a Local **Stable Audio 3 Small SFX** model on CPU (free, \~7–10s per 4s clip after model load). My laptop doesn't have a discrete GPU, so you should be able to do this on any hardware - no graphics card needed. 

The big difference is that Gemini can listen back to the files and self-assess, whereas Claude could only look at the wavelengths and such. Gemini also wrote a more layered prompt, whereas Claude was essentially trying to brute force it with a more simplistic generator. 

I'm happy to share a more detailed explanation (which will be directly copied/pasted from AI, if you're cool with that) so you can replicate the pipeline. 

Claude did OK with the more abstract sound effects, but when it came to animal sounds (critical for my game) it just completely whiffed. Gemini hit it within 1-2 tries. 

I then had Gemini go back and listen to the 75 sounds that Claude had originally built, and it only suggested to replace 5, which I felt pretty good about. 

I then had Claude write up a plan to wire the sounds in, and used Gemini 4 Neon High for most of that work - I honestly trust Claude much more with the code, but needed to save my Claude tokens for another project, so I felt comfortable letting Claude write the plan and then letting Gemini execute it. 

The game is [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.drywater.game](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.drywater.game) if you want to check it out.

comments.author: MaqeSweden
comments.body:
Scope creep!

When adding new features or expanding a map is so easy, it's very difficult to stay focused on just game mechanics. I find myself about 20% in to a quite huge game, and only just now realizing I have to put effort into making the first few hours actually playable and fun for actual players.

and when the game is already that big, all small decisions become unnecessarily big decisions.

That, and making actually good realistic 3d-models. And deciding what's good enough.

comments.author: richchiudev
comments.body:
>Beyond tuning game feel (which is definitely huge), the biggest surprise for me was **multiplayer state syncing and regressions**.  
Getting individual features working was super fast, but once multiple players interact simultaneously, AI struggles to keep track of edge cases across different scripts. Half the time, asking it to fix one desync issue accidentally breaks a mechanic that was working fine five minutes ago. Keeping the codebase modular and testing every tiny change myself became way more important than I expected!
